title: The system design method, worked on Ticketmaster
subtitle: A repeatable five-step method for a 45-minute design interview, worked through on a ticket booking system like Ticketmaster.

c.v: On 15 November 2022, Ticketmaster opened a presale for Taylor Swift's Eras Tour. Over 3.5 million people had pre-registered as Verified Fans. About 1.5 million of them got codes to join the sale. The other 2 million were put on a waiting list.
On the day, Ticketmaster says, "the staggering number of bot attacks" and fans without codes drove huge traffic. The site got 3.5 billion total system requests, four times its previous peak.

To keep the systems up, it slowed down some sales and pushed others back. Fans waited longer in the queue. Ticketmaster estimates that about 15% of interactions on the site had issues. Some fans lost tickets they had already put in their cart, because codes failed to validate.
Over 2 million tickets were still sold that day.
Two days later, Ticketmaster cancelled the general public sale. The reason it gave was "extraordinarily high demands on ticketing systems and insufficient remaining ticket inventory".
Hello Interview has a full worked answer for "design Ticketmaster".
The story shows why the problem is hard. It tests the whole method: what to build, what must never go wrong, and what happens when demand is far bigger than supply.
A system design interview is a conversation of about 45 minutes about a big, vague problem.
There is no single right answer. The interviewer wants to see how you think: how you clarify the problem, choose a design and explain trade-offs.

Without a method, people start drawing the parts of the system right away. Twenty minutes later, they find they solved the wrong problem. A method gives you a path, and it lets you lead the conversation.
Hello Interview's framework has five main steps, plus an optional data flow step that we skip here.
Alex Xu's book uses four steps that cover the same ground: understand the problem, propose a high-level design,
deep dive
, and wrap up.
The key idea.
First agree on what to build. Then build the simplest design that works. Then spend your best time on the parts that are hard. Each step leaves an artefact on the board that the next step uses.
Step through the five steps for a ticket booking system, with what each one puts on the board. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Step 1. Requirements (about 5 minutes)
Split them into two lists.
Functional requirements
are what users can do.
Non-functional requirements
are the qualities the system must have, such as speed, scale and consistency. Hello Interview advises picking the top 3 functional ones.
For Ticketmaster, the breakdown chooses three: view events, search for events, and book tickets.
The key non-functional ones are:
Consistency for booking.
No seat is ever sold twice.
Availability
for search and viewing.
Slightly old data is fine here.
Scale for popular events.
For example, 10 million users for one event.
Fast search
, under 500 ms. Reads far outnumber writes, about 100 to 1.
Say out loud what is out of
scope
, for example dynamic pricing or an admin tool. Xu's first rule is to ask, not assume.
Back-of-envelope numbers
Do maths only where it changes the design.
Here it does. The 10 million comes from the breakdown.
The other numbers are our own guesses, so label them as guesses in the interview:
10 million fans arrive in the first 10 minutes. That is 10,000,000 ÷ 600 s ≈
17,000 new users per second
Each one reloads the seat map about 10 times in those 10 minutes. That is roughly
170,000 reads per second
on one event.
A stadium has about 70,000 seats. So at most 70,000 bookings can succeed, while millions of people try.
The lesson from the numbers: reads need caching, and the write path needs a gate in front. See
latency numbers and estimation
for the method.
Step 2. Core entities (about 2 minutes)
List the main nouns. Do not design every column yet.
For Ticketmaster: Event, User, Venue (with its seat map), Performer, Ticket (one per seat, with a status) and Booking (one order of tickets).
Step 3. API (about 5 minutes)
Write one endpoint per main user action. Hello Interview suggests REST, plain HTTP endpoints such as
GET /events/{id}
, unless you have a reason not to. Take the user from the login token, not from the request body.

blocks.v:
GET  /events/search?keyword=&start=&end=&page=   → Event[]
GET  /events/:eventId                            → Event, Venue, Performer, Ticket[]
POST /bookings/:eventId  { ticketIds, paymentDetails }  → bookingId

c.v: These follow the breakdown's own API.
Step 4. High-level design (10–15 minutes)
Draw the simplest design that meets the functional requirements.
Clients reach an
API gateway
. Behind it sit an event service, a search service and a booking service. The breakdown keeps bookings and tickets in one Postgres database, so a
transaction
can update both. A payment provider takes the money.
Stay simple here. When you see a problem, name it and say you will come back to it.
Step 5. Deep dives (about 10 minutes)
Now go back to the hard non-functional requirements. Each deep dive should answer one.
Holding a seat during payment.
Payment can take minutes. Holding a database lock that long is a bad idea. It ties up database resources and raises the risk of
deadlocks
Instead, put a hold on the seat that expires on its own. The breakdown uses Redis with a 10-minute
TTL
In Redis,
SET seat:42 user7 NX EX 600
sets the key only if it does not exist yet, and it expires after 600 seconds.
The docs advise a random token as the value, so a client can only delete its own lock.
Two warnings make a senior answer. The Redis docs discourage this simple lock pattern in favour of their Redlock algorithm.
And the database must still be the final check when the seat is sold. Use the conditional update from
inventory and flash sales
. Make the payment step safe to
retry
, as in
idempotency, retries and timeouts
Surviving the surge.
Put a
virtual waiting room
in front of seat selection. In the breakdown, users join a queue and are let in from the front, from time to time or as tickets sell. The booking service rejects users who were not let in.
Products exist for this. Cloudflare's Waiting Room admits visitors by a limit on total active users and on new users per minute. Others wait in first-in-first-out order and see an estimated wait.
Add
rate limiting
per user to slow down bots.
Fast search and seat maps.
Use a search index instead of
LIKE '%…%'
queries on the database.
Cache
event and venue data, which rarely change, with long TTLs. Cache seat availability only with a short TTL.
See
caching and cache stampedes
Timeboxing and driving
Keep a clock in view. If requirements take 15 minutes, you will have no time for deep dives. Talk while you think. Xu warns: "Don't think in silence."

Lead the conversation, but check with the interviewer. Say "I plan to go deep on the seat hold next. Is that where you want to spend time?" Hello Interview says senior candidates should find the hard parts and lead the deep dives. It also says to give the interviewer room to ask questions.
Its breakdown expects a senior to go deep on topics such as a
distributed lock
for holds, and to explain trade-offs. A mid-level answer can use a simpler fix, such as a ticket status with a
timeout
Database lock held during payment
Locks last minutes, tie up the database and risk deadlocks.
Avoid for long user steps.
Ticket status with an expiry time, checked in short transactions
Simple. Expired holds need a cleanup job, or a check at read time.
Most systems, and a solid mid-level answer.
Redis hold with a TTL, plus a final database check
One more system to run.
Big on-sales with many holds per second.
Virtual waiting room
Not directly. It limits load.
Fans wait, and you must keep the queue fair.
Known surges, such as a big presale.
Showing live seat maps to everyone
It only shows state.
Heavy reads, and maps go stale in seconds.
Normal events. Hide them behind the queue for huge ones.
Simple rule:
make the database the final judge of who gets a seat. Use holds and the waiting room to keep the load on the database low.

sections.name: At work
sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: The same method runs a good design review at work. Only the clock changes, from 45 minutes to a few weeks.
Start every
design doc
with functional and non-functional requirements, and a list of
non-goals
. See
design docs and RFCs
Ask for the numbers that change the design: peak users, reads to writes, data size. Write the assumptions down.
In a review, ask the author:
"Which requirement does this part serve?"
A box with no requirement is extra cost.
Spend review time on the riskiest parts, not on naming or the parts everyone agrees on.
For each deep dive, ask for two options and why one was chosen.
Before launch, ask what happens at 4 times the expected peak. Ticketmaster's presale reached four times its previous peak.
"Act as a system design interviewer. Ask me to design a ticket booking system, then stop me if I skip requirements or run over time on any step."
"Here are my requirements and my design for seat booking. List every way two users could end up with the same seat, and which part of my design stops each one."
"Check my back-of-envelope estimate: 10 million users in 10 minutes, 10 seat-map reads each. Show each step with units."
Every part of the design maps to a requirement you wrote first.
The agent did not quietly add requirements or skip the non-functional ones.
Double booking is stopped by the database, not only by a cache or a lock that can expire.
Numbers come with units and labelled assumptions. Agents often state guesses as facts.
You can explain every trade-off in your own words. An interviewer will ask "why?"

q.v: The interviewer says "Design Ticketmaster." What should you do in the first five minutes?

options.v: Draw the services and databases you will need.
Agree on the top functional requirements and the key non-functional ones, such as no double booking.
Start with the hardest part, the seat lock.

why.v: Requirements decide everything that follows. Without them you may design the wrong system, or spend your time on parts nobody asked for.

q.v: Which requirement is the main reason the booking path needs strong consistency?

options.v: Search must return results in under 500 ms.
Two people must never buy the same seat.

why.v: Search can show slightly old data, but a seat sold twice is a real failure. So booking chooses consistency and search chooses availability.

q.v: A user picks a seat and starts paying, which can take minutes. What is the best way to stop another user from buying it, without tying up the database?

options.v: A hold on the seat that expires after a set time, such as 10 minutes.
A database lock held until payment finishes.
Nothing. The first payment to finish wins.

why.v: A hold with a TTL keeps the seat for one user and frees it on its own if they leave. A database lock held for minutes ties up the database and raises the risk of deadlocks.

q.v: Ten million fans arrive for one event at the same minute. Which part protects the booking service most directly?

options.v: A bigger cache for event pages.
A virtual waiting room that admits users at a rate the system can handle.

why.v: The waiting room limits how many people reach seat selection and booking at once. Caching helps reads, but not the write rush.

q.v: You have 10 minutes left and your high-level design works. What is the best use of the time?

options.v: Go deep on the hardest non-functional requirement and explain the trade-offs.

why.v: Deep dives show seniority. They prove the design meets the hard requirements, and they show you can compare options.
